title: Backcasting a 'Provable Limit on Hiding': Empirically Probing What a Model Cannot Conceal in Its Activations

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting a 'Provable Limit on Hiding': Empirically Probing What a Model Cannot Conceal in Its Activations

**Problem:** Success state (UK AISI Alignment Project): we can prove theoretical limits on what an AI can hide about its behavior. A concrete empirical instantiation: the quirky-models finding that the latent representation of a concealed token 'flares up' in middle layers even under training to deny it. The gap is whether this concealment-leakage is universal across concealment types or specific to the keyword setup.

**Direction:** On open models, fine-tune-free: prompt small instruction models to deliberately conceal a known fact (via system prompt), then probe activations for the concealed content with simple linear probes. Test several concealment instructions and fact types. Measure whether leakage is consistent — i.e., whether there's an empirical 'you can't hide it in the residual stream' regularity.

**Why it matters:** Working backward from a proven hiding-limit theorem, we need empirical regularities the theorem could formalize. Showing concealment robustly leaks (or sometimes doesn't) tells theorists what to try to prove and gives a practical detector — all on open models.

**Relevant context:** ELK quirky-models: secret-token representations flare up in middle layers even under training to conceal; UK AISI Alignment Project open problem on limits of hiding.
